name: fuath

attributes.attribute: spectral monster of Highland Gaelic folklore tied to water
Scottish Gaelic etymology hatred or aversion
Old Irish cognate fuath for hate and likeness

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The fuath names a group of spirit beings drawn from Highland Gaelic folk tradition. The Scottish Gaelic root carries the sense of aversion. Old Irish attests a cognate form for hate and likeness. These beings most often haunt waters, lochs, rivers, and the open sea. Some sources call the same beings arrachd or fuath-arrachd. A fuath gives birth to the brollachan. The Highland varieties include the beithir, the fideal, the peallaidh, and the ùruisg. The spelling vough is a phonetic anglicization. Related figures appear under arrach and glastig. Folklorists list motifs F420.5.2 and F470.

okr.objective: Anchor fuath as a Highland Gaelic water-monster class with subspecies and folk motifs.
key_results: Give the Scottish Gaelic etymology for fuath.
Name water, lochs, rivers, and the sea as the fuath haunts.
Record arrachd and fuath-arrachd as alternate names.
List beithir, fideal, peallaidh, and ùruisg as subspecies.
Note the brollachan as the offspring of a fuath.
Mark vough as a phonetic anglicization.
Assign folk motifs F420.5.2 and F470.
